subject: math
domain: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability
cluster: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
intro: The conditional probability of $A$ given $B$ is $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$, defined whenever $P(B)>0$. It measures how likely $A$ is once you restrict attention to the outcomes where $B$ has happened. These problems ramp from direct substitution to extracting values from tables and Venn diagrams, then to rearranging the rule and testing independence by checking whether $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$.

items.prompt: In a club of $40$ members, $24$ play chess. Among the chess players, $9$ are left-handed. Given that a randomly chosen member plays chess, find the probability that the member is left-handed, $P(\text{left-handed}\mid\text{chess})$.

steps: Conditioning on chess restricts the sample space to the $24$ chess players.

items.prompt: A fair six-sided die is rolled. Let $A=\{\text{prime}\}=\{2,3,5\}$ and $B=\{\text{odd}\}=\{1,3,5\}$. Find $P(A\mid B)$.

steps: Conditioning on $B$ restricts the outcomes to the odd numbers $\{1,3,5\}$, which has $3$ outcomes.
Among those, the primes are $A\cap B=\{3,5\}$, which has $2$ outcomes.

items.prompt: A survey of $90$ commuters records mode of travel and whether they own a bicycle. $36$ commuters own a bicycle; of those, $27$ ride the bus. Given that a commuter owns a bicycle, find the probability that the commuter rides the bus.

steps: Let $A=\text{rides the bus}$ and $B=\text{owns a bicycle}$; we want $P(A\mid B)$.
Conditioning on owning a bicycle restricts to the $36$ bicycle owners.
Of those, $27$ ride the bus, so $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{27}{36}$.

items.prompt: A two-way table classifies $50$ students by whether they passed an exam (Pass / Fail) and whether they studied (Studied / Did not study). The cell counts are: Studied & Pass $=18$, Studied & Fail $=2$, Did not study & Pass $=12$, Did not study & Fail $=18$. Given that a randomly chosen student studied, find the probability that the student passed.

steps: Find the total who studied: $18+2=20$ students.

items.prompt: From a two-way table, $P(A\text{ and }B)=\dfrac{12}{50}$, $P(A)=\dfrac{20}{50}$, and $P(B)=\dfrac{15}{50}$. Compute both $P(A\mid B)$ and $P(B\mid A)$, and state whether they are equal.
items.answer: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{4}{5}$ and $P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{3}{5}$; they are not equal

steps: Since $\dfrac{4}{5}\ne\dfrac{3}{5}$, the two conditional probabilities are not equal: conditioning on $B$ is different from conditioning on $A$.

items.prompt: Given $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{3}{4}$ and $P(B)=\dfrac{2}{5}$, find the joint probability $P(A\text{ and }B)$.

steps: Rearrange the definition $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\text{ and }B)}{P(B)}$ to solve for the joint probability: $P(A\text{ and }B)=P(A\mid B)\,P(B)$.

items.prompt: In a Venn diagram for events $A$ and $B$ over $60$ equally likely outcomes, the region only $A$ contains $14$ outcomes, the overlap $A\cap B$ contains $10$ outcomes, the region only $B$ contains $15$ outcomes, and the outside region contains $21$ outcomes. Find $P(A\mid B)$.

steps: Event $B$ consists of the overlap plus only-$B$: $10+15=25$ outcomes, so $P(B)=\dfrac{25}{60}$.
The outcomes in both $A$ and $B$ are the overlap: $A\cap B=10$, so $P(A\text{ and }B)=\dfrac{10}{60}$.

items.prompt: Given $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{3}$, $P(B)=\dfrac{1}{2}$, and $P(A\text{ and }B)=\dfrac{1}{6}$, determine whether $A$ and $B$ are independent. Justify your answer using conditional probability.

steps: Independence holds exactly when $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$. Here $P(A)=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
Since $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{1}{3}=P(A)$, knowing $B$ occurred does not change the probability of $A$.

items.prompt: A two-way table of $200$ people classifies them by whether they exercise regularly ($E$) and whether they have low blood pressure ($L$): $E$ and $L=60$, $E$ and not $L=20$, not $E$ and $L=60$, not $E$ and not $L=60$. Determine whether exercising regularly and having low blood pressure are independent, justifying with a conditional probability.
items.answer: They are not independent (they are dependent), because $P(L\mid E)=\dfrac{3}{4}\ne\dfrac{3}{5}=P(L)$

steps: Total with low blood pressure: $60+60=120$, so $P(L)=\dfrac{120}{200}=\dfrac{3}{5}$.
Independence requires $P(L\mid E)=P(L)$. Here $\dfrac{3}{4}\ne\dfrac{3}{5}$, so exercising raises the chance of low blood pressure. Thus $E$ and $L$ are not independent (they are dependent).

items.prompt: At a school, $P(\text{plays an instrument})=\dfrac{2}{5}$ and $P(\text{sings in choir}\mid\text{plays an instrument})=\dfrac{1}{4}$. Find the probability that a randomly chosen student both plays an instrument and sings in choir, then express that joint probability as a percent.

steps: Let $I=\text{plays an instrument}$ and $S=\text{sings in choir}$. Use $P(S\text{ and }I)=P(S\mid I)\,P(I)$.
So $10\%$ of students both play an instrument and sing in choir.

items.prompt: A box has $25$ marbles. $10$ are red, and the rest are blue. Of the red marbles, $6$ are chipped; of the blue marbles, $3$ are chipped. A marble is drawn at random. Compute $P(\text{chipped}\mid\text{red})$ and $P(\text{red}\mid\text{chipped})$, and explain why these two conditional probabilities differ.
items.answer: $P(\text{chipped}\mid\text{red})=\dfrac{3}{5}$ and $P(\text{red}\mid\text{chipped})=\dfrac{2}{3}$; they differ because they condition on different events

steps: There are $10$ red and $15$ blue marbles; chipped marbles total $6+3=9$.
$P(\text{chipped}\mid\text{red})$ restricts to the $10$ red marbles, of which $6$ are chipped: $\dfrac{6}{10}=\dfrac{3}{5}$.
$P(\text{red}\mid\text{chipped})$ restricts to the $9$ chipped marbles, of which $6$ are red: $\dfrac{6}{9}=\dfrac{2}{3}$.
The values differ because the conditioning event (the restricted sample space) is different: one divides by the $10$ red marbles, the other by the $9$ chipped marbles.

items.prompt: In a town, $P(\text{rain})=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(\text{traffic jam}\mid\text{rain})=\dfrac{3}{5}$, while $P(\text{traffic jam})=\dfrac{1}{5}$. First find $P(\text{rain and traffic jam})$, then determine whether rain and traffic jams are independent, justifying your conclusion.
items.answer: $P(\text{rain and traffic jam})=\dfrac{3}{20}$; they are not independent because $P(\text{traffic jam}\mid\text{rain})=\dfrac{3}{5}\ne\dfrac{1}{5}=P(\text{traffic jam})$

steps: Let $R=\text{rain}$ and $T=\text{traffic jam}$. Recover the joint probability: $P(R\text{ and }T)=P(T\mid R)\,P(R)=\dfrac{3}{5}\cdot\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{3}{20}$.
Since $\dfrac{3}{5}\ne\dfrac{1}{5}$, rain raises the chance of a traffic jam, so $R$ and $T$ are not independent (they are dependent).
